title: "Dead Ends?"
body-classes: page-small
---

Work that has not reached publication: analyses that stalled, manuscripts that
were drafted and shelved, and tools I built and stopped using. Where results
exist I report them, including the null ones. The published record makes
research look far tidier than it is.

::: {.topic}
## Emotion regulation in early childhood

Secondary analyses of existing longitudinal datasets, mostly asking whether
physiological and behavioural regulation can be described jointly rather than
separately.
:::

### Profiles of regulation strategies and physiological reactivity

[Analysed, not written up]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Rather than treating strategy use and physiology as separate predictors,
describe each child by a *profile* combining observed regulation strategies,
baseline RSA, and RSA reactivity within a task. Then ask what predicts profile
membership (for instance whether maternal depression predicts less help-seeking)
and how profiles relate to problem behaviour.
:::

::: {.field}
[Measures]{.k}

Observed strategies coded per task: hostility, physical strategies,
help-seeking, disengagement, and persistence in one cohort; help-seeking,
distraction, physical negative, verbal negative, and resignation in the other.
Baseline RSA and RSA reactivity per task.
:::

### Attention as a vulnerability factor

[Analysed. Moderation not supported]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Whether attentional difficulty acts as a vulnerability that amplifies the
effect of social risk on behaviour problems, as a moderated mediation.
:::

::: {.field}
[Results]{.k}

The moderation did not hold. In the first model (N = 199) social risk predicted
total problems strongly (b = 10.87, p &lt; .001) but the interaction with
attention did not (b = 13.68, p = .227). Simple slopes told the same story:
significant only at the middle of the moderator (b = 17.50, p = .009), not at
low (p = .056) or high (p = .065) values, which is the pattern you get when an
interaction is not really there. A second model (N = 375) added a behavioural
attention measure and none of the attention terms reached significance
(attention b = 16.10, p = .137; attention × behaviour b = −18.26, p = .104;
baseline RSA b = −3.39, p = .530). Social risk remained the only reliable
predictor (b = 9.80, p &lt; .001).
:::

### Developmental trajectory of emotion regulation, ages 4 to 10

[Models fitted, not written up]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Describe the shape of change in observed emotion regulation across early and
middle childhood, and test whether children follow distinguishable trajectory
classes.
:::

::: {.field}
[Analysis]{.k}

Latent growth curve models in Mplus on emotion regulation at ages 4, 5, 7, and
10 (N = 398): linear, quadratic, and growth mixture specifications.
:::

::: {.field}
[Results]{.k}

Mean growth was positive but very small (slope 0.029 on the observed scale), and
the variance around it was smaller still (0.004), meaning there was little
individual difference in change for later models to explain. That is the main
reason the mixture extension went nowhere.
:::

### Profiles of RSA reactivity across emotion-eliciting contexts

[Designed for a special issue, not completed]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Most work treats RSA reactivity as one quantity. I wanted to compare reactivity
across tasks designed to elicit different emotions, profile children on that
pattern, compare profiles across age groups, and relate them to other
self-regulation measures.
:::

::: {.field}
[Measures]{.k}

Fear (jumping spider), frustration (toy in a box), and positive (bubbles) tasks
at ages 2 and 4; positive surprise (snake) and frustration (candy) tasks at age
5. A parallel question compared reactivity during mother-directed problem
solving against child-independent tasks, as a way of watching co-regulation
become independent regulation.
:::

### A network of physiological regulation, self-regulation, and behaviour

[Proposed, not run]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Estimate a psychometric network across regulation domains (emotional,
behavioural, cognitive, attentional) together with physiological regulation,
separately by age group, and if the data allowed, as a temporal network.
Adaptive and maladaptive outcomes would enter as additional nodes rather than
as separate outcome models.
:::

### Reactivity and sensitivity as antecedents of regulation

[Data assembled, analysis incomplete]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Whether infant reactivity and maternal sensitivity measured in the first years
predict later emotion regulation, and whether sensitivity moderates the effect
of reactivity.
:::

::: {.topic}
## Teacher and child physiological synchrony

Four manuscripts drafted from one classroom observation study. I am no longer an
author on the parent project; these entries record the analyses I did.
:::

### Synchrony and teacher communication

[Analysed, drafted]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Analysis]{.k}

Dyadic models estimated with a Bayesian estimator, controlling for child age,
gender, and race, relating teacher-child physiological synchrony to observed
communication.
:::

### RSA inertia

[Analysis started]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Carry inertia, the tendency of a physiological state to persist, from the affect
dynamics literature into classroom RSA, as an individual difference rather than
a nuisance parameter.
:::

### Second-by-second synchrony

[Analysis started]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Whether coupling estimated at the second level, rather than in 30-second epochs,
recovers structure that epoching averages away.
:::

### Physiological and behavioural regulation

[Analysed with GIMME]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Analysis]{.k}

Group Iterative Multiple Model Estimation, recovering group-level and
individual-level directed paths between physiological and behavioural
regulation rather than assuming one model fits every dyad.
:::

::: {.topic}
## Adolescent stress and emotion dynamics
:::

### Emotion dynamics linking academic adversity to internalizing symptoms

[Poster at ISSBD 2026, Incheon. Manuscript paused]{.status}

The result I did not predict is the interesting one. Patterns usually called
maladaptive looked protective under adversity: low negative-affect
differentiation buffered cumulative stress on anxiety, high negative-affect
instability buffered immediate stress on both depression and anxiety, and low
positive-affect inertia was protective against immediate stress on anxiety.
Negative-affect intensity behaved as expected, mediating stress to both
outcomes.

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Whether emotion dynamics are the adaptation process connecting academic stress
to internalizing symptoms, through two competing routes: coping with adversity
drains the resources regulation requires, or adaptive regulation buffers the
stressor. Four dynamics: intensity, instability, inertia, and differentiation.
:::

::: {.field}
[Analysis]{.k}

Dynamic structural equation modelling to derive person-level dynamic indices,
then structural models testing mediation and moderation, with a sensitivity
battery run alongside.
:::

::: {.field}
[Participants]{.k}

271 adolescents in a longitudinal study in the southern United States, 38% in
7th grade and 62% in 8th, 56% female. 47% Latinx, 19% White, 11% Asian, 5%
Black, 18% other.
:::

::: {.field}
[Measures]{.k}

Three annual surveys measuring cumulative academic stress and depressive and
anxiety symptoms, and a daily diary measuring daily academic stress and positive
and negative affect.
:::

::: {.topic}
## Coursework

Doctoral course projects that were done properly but were never meant to become
papers. Two produced clean null results.
:::

### Bidirectional relations between peer relationships and emotion regulation

[Final paper, structural equation modelling course]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Whether peer relationship quality and emotion regulation predict each other over
time, rather than one being prior to the other. Fitted as a cross-lagged
structural model.
:::

### Developmental trajectory of social skills

[Term project, longitudinal analysis course]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

I predicted social skills would follow a nonlinear trajectory: growth from early
to middle childhood, then a plateau or decline in adolescence. I also expected
physiological regulation to predict the rate of growth.
:::

::: {.field}
[Results]{.k}

Both predictions failed. Growth was linear and positive (b = 0.014, SE = 0.001,
p &lt; .001), and the quadratic term was not significant (b = −0.001, SE = 0.0004,
p = .067), so social skills kept improving into adolescence rather than
levelling off. The interaction between physiological regulation and time was
also null (b = −0.012, SE = 0.015, p = .395). Between-person differences were
large (ICC = .66), so most of the variance was in where children started rather
than how they changed.
:::

[Seminar proposal]{.status}

::: {.field}

A grant-style proposal written for a doctoral seminar on the neuroscience of

::: {.topic}
## Tools
:::

### An automated literature-review pipeline

[Version 1.0, unmaintained]{.status}

::: {.field}
[Idea]{.k}

Screening for a systematic review is mechanical and error-prone in a way that
seemed automatable: take exported search results, fill the metadata gaps, and
triage abstracts against inclusion criteria so a human only adjudicates the
ambiguous ones.
:::

::: {.field}
[Built]{.k}

An R pipeline that ingested CSV exports from LitSift, combined them across
searches, and recovered missing abstracts from the CrossRef API by DOI, with
per-record error handling so one bad response could not kill a run. It reached
metadata completion and stopped before screening, which is the part that
matters. General-purpose agents now close that gap.
:::
